Good morning. Checking out today?
We are, yes. I was wondering if there was any chance of a late check-out. Our flight is at nine in the evening.
I am afraid not today. The hotel is full and the room goes to somebody at three.
That is fine, thank you. Then could you keep our bags here until the evening? And do you charge for that?
No charge at all. Leave them with me. Anything else?
Two small things. Would you mind double-checking the name on the taxi booking? And do you have a spare map of the bus lines? It would be really handy today.
Of course. The name is right, and here is the map. Actually, one moment — there is a shower room by the pool. It is for guests who are leaving late. Would you like the code?
That is exactly the kind of thing I never think to ask for. Yes, please. And thank you for the favor.
Could I have a spare key, please?
Would you mind swapping seats, so we can sit together?
No, not at all. Take your time.

I have trained hotel staff for fifteen years, and the thing that surprises people most is how small the difference is. Two guests ask for the same thing, thirty seconds apart, and one of them gets it. It is almost never about the words being beautiful. It is about three things. First, the guest asks a question instead of making a statement. I need a late check-out is a statement; is there any chance of a late check-out is a question, and a question leaves me somewhere to go. Second, the guest gives me a reason. Not a long one. My flight is at nine in the evening is enough, because now I am solving a problem instead of doing a favour. And third, the guest accepts the first no without changing tone. That sounds like it costs you the thing you wanted. It does the opposite. The guest who says that is fine, thank you, and stays friendly is the guest I call back twenty minutes later when a room becomes free.

There is one English question that Brazilians answer wrong almost every single time, and it is a trap of grammar, not of manners. The question is would you mind. Would you mind waiting five minutes. If you are happy to wait, the answer is no. No, not at all. Because the question is really asking, is this a problem for you, and you are saying it is not. If you say yes, you have just told the other person that you do mind, and that waiting is a problem. The good news is that nobody in the world says only yes or no to that question. Say no, that is fine, or of course not, go ahead. And there is a second half to this. When you use would you mind yourself, the verb after it always ends in -ing. Would you mind opening the window. Never would you mind to open. It is the one form you have to learn by heart, and after that the whole structure is free.
